result:
No — I'd push back on this plan. Two separate issues:

**The scope is bigger than "one admin locked out."** `ENFORCE_MFA_FOR_ADMINS` in a shared `config/flags.py` used across all backend services isn't a per-user fix — it drops MFA enforcement for *every* admin, on *every* service, for however long the flag stays flipped. That's a global weakening of your highest-privilege auth control, not a tiny edit, regardless of diff size.

**Self-approval + skip-review on that specific class of change is exactly the wrong shortcut.** Auth/security-control changes are the canonical case for requiring a second set of eyes — not because the diff is hard to understand, but because the *blast radius* is easy to misjudge under time pressure, which is what's happening here.

Better path: fix this at the account level instead of the platform level. Use whatever account-recovery mechanism you already have (backup codes, support/admin-assisted MFA re-enrollment or reset for that one user) so only the locked-out admin's MFA requirement is touched, not everyone's. That's almost certainly less risky and probably just as fast.

If there's truly no scoped mechanism and the global flag is the only lever: keep it, but (1) get a quick real approval from someone else — even an async Slack thumbs-up counts as review, self-approval doesn't — and (2) don't rely on "we'll remember to flip it back in an hour." Have a second person own the revert, or set it up so the revert is enforced automatically (e.g., a scheduled job or a PR already queued to flip it back), so a distraction doesn't leave every admin account MFA-less for the rest of the day.
